chunks: Common-mode vs differential gain, CMRR. The question: What is common-mode and differential gain? What are their ideal values?
A differential amplifier is meant to amplify the difference between two inputs and ignore what they have in common.
The "common-mode" part is the average of the two inputs, which is often noise. The common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR) says how well the amplifier ignores that average.
Imagine two people carrying a tray on a bumpy bus. The tray tilts only if they lift unevenly. If both rise and fall together, the tray stays level.
A good amplifier is like a tray that reacts only to the uneven lift. A real one is a bit wobbly, so some of the shared bump leaks through.
V 2 goes to the non-inverting input through the R 3 over R 4 divider and V 1 to the inverting input.
If R 4 over R 3 equals R 2 over R 1 equals 10 the circuit amplifies V 2-V 1 by 10 and exactly cancels any common-mode voltage.
Differential voltage ( V d ): the difference between the two inputs. Common-mode voltage ( V cm ): the average of the two inputs.
Differential gain ( A d ): how much the difference is amplified. Op-amps ("What an op-amp is and how it works") are the usual building block.
Common-mode gain ( A cm ): how much the average leaks to the output. Ideally zero. CMRR: the ratio A d over A cm . Higher is better.
Often given in decibels (dB), where every 20 decibels is another factor of 10.
Say the inputs are 5. 001 volts and 4. 999 volts. The difference is 2 millivolts and the average is 5 volts. An amplifier with A d equals 10 should output 20 millivolts.
An ideal one ignores the 5 volts average. A real one with CMRR of 100 decibels, which is a ratio of 100,000, has A cm equals 10 over 100 000 equals 0. 0001 , so it adds 5 times 0.
0001 equals 0. 5 millivolts of error to the 20 millivolts. Build the same gain from four 1% resistors, though, and the CMRR can fall to about 275 (49 decibels).
Then the 5 volts average adds about 180 millivolts, swamping the signal. That is the whole idea.
"Split two inputs into a difference and an average.
Differential gain is the gain on the difference and common-mode gain is the gain on the average, so the output is A dV d plus A cmV cm .
Ideally A d is large (or the designed gain) and A cm is zero, so the common-mode rejection ratio A d over A cm is infinite.

In practice mismatch leaves a small A cm : a four-resistor difference amp with 1% resistors and a gain of 10 has a worst-case CMRR of about 275, or 49 decibels, which is why precision designs use matched networks or instrumentation amps."
